{"D683/ch1/s1": {"title": "ML Refresher: Where Advanced ML Begins", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
BiasError from oversimplified assumptions; underfitting.
VarianceError from sensitivity to training noise; overfitting.
GeneralizationA model's ability to perform on unseen data.
HyperparameterSetting chosen before training (e.g., tree depth) — distinct from learned parameters.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — the bias-variance checkpoint before advanced ML

WORKED EXAMPLE — diagnose three models at a glance
Same dataset, three fits:
• Model A: train error 22%, val error 23% → both high → high bias (underfit): model too simple → add capacity/features.
• Model B: train 1%, val 19% → big gap → high variance (overfit): regularize, more data, simpler model.
• Model C: train 5%, val 7% → healthy → ship the pipeline forward.
Advanced ML is largely industrialized responses to this table: ensembles and regularization attack variance; deeper architectures and better features attack bias. If you can read train/val curves, every later chapter has a place to hang.
⚠️ THE GAP IS THE DIAGNOSIS
Both-high → bias. Gap → variance. This two-line rule is assumed everywhere in D683 — questions quote error pairs and expect the word.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Advanced ML doesn't start with new algorithms — it starts with knowing exactly where simple ones break. If you can't articulate why a linear model fails on certain problems, you can't motivate the leap to ensembles, deep learning, or transformers.

Core concepts

1. Supervised vs unsupervised. Supervised learning maps inputs to known labels (regression, classification). Unsupervised finds structure without labels (clustering, dim reduction). Most production ML is supervised — you generally have or can collect labels.

2. The bias-variance tradeoff. Bias is error from oversimplified assumptions; variance is sensitivity to training noise. High bias underfits, high variance overfits. Every model decision pushes one up and the other down.

3. Where classical ML fails. Linear models fail on non-linear relationships. Trees overfit. KNN dies in high dimensions. Naive Bayes assumes independence that rarely holds. Each failure motivates an advanced technique.

4. Why ensembles bridge gaps. Combining many imperfect models smooths individual errors. Bagging cuts variance (Random Forest). Boosting cuts both bias and variance (XGBoost). The whole reliably beats any part.

5. When advanced ML helps. Advanced techniques shine on high-dimensional data, non-linear interactions, image/text/audio inputs, and low-signal regimes. Not every problem needs them — start simple.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Reaching for deep learning when a Random Forest would do — tree ensembles often beat NNs on small/medium tabular data.
  • Ignoring the bias-variance lens — picking 'the most complex' model rather than the right one.
  • Confusing 'no labels' with 'unsupervised problem' — often you can label cheaply and convert to supervised.

Quick recap

Advanced ML extends classical ML by addressing specific failure modes: high variance (ensembles), non-linearity (deep learning), sequence structure (RNNs/Transformers), unstructured input (CNNs, embeddings). The bias-variance tradeoff is your North Star.

Glossary

Bias
Error from oversimplified assumptions; underfitting.
Variance
Error from sensitivity to training noise; overfitting.
Generalization
A model's ability to perform on unseen data.
Hyperparameter
Setting chosen before training (e.g., tree depth) — distinct from learned parameters.
"}, "D683/ch1/s2": {"title": "Ensemble Methods: Bagging, Boosting, Stacking", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
Bootstrap sampleSampling with replacement from training data.
Out-of-fold predictionPrediction made on a held-out fold during cross-validation.
Early stoppingHalting training when validation metric stops improving.
Weak learnerA model only slightly better than chance; building block for boosting.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — bagging, boosting, stacking mechanically

WORKED EXAMPLE — the same 3 learners, three combinators
• Bagging: 200 trees, each trained on a bootstrap resample (+ random feature subsets = random forest), predictions averaged/voted — parallel, cuts VARIANCE.
• Boosting: learner 2 trains on learner 1’s residuals/mistakes, learner 3 on learner 2’s… (gradient boosting/XGBoost) — sequential, cuts BIAS, usually top score on tabular data.
• Stacking: forest + boosting + logistic each predict; a META-model learns from their outputs which to trust where.
Numbers from a churn run: single tree F1 0.71 → forest 0.79 → XGBoost 0.82 → stack 0.83. Diminishing returns, rising complexity — the honest trade to report.
⚠️ STACKING NEEDS CLEAN FOLDS
The meta-model must train on OUT-OF-FOLD predictions of the base models; training it on their in-sample predictions leaks and inflates. That subtlety is the advanced-course question.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Ensembles consistently win Kaggle competitions and production tabular ML. Random Forest and XGBoost beat sophisticated single models because errors made by one are corrected by others. Knowing which ensemble fits which problem separates intermediate from advanced practitioners.

Core concepts

1. Bagging. Train many models on bootstrap samples; average predictions. Random Forest is bagging applied to decision trees plus random feature subsets at each split. Reduces variance.

2. Boosting. Train models sequentially, each focusing on errors of previous ones. Gradient Boosting fits new trees to residuals. AdaBoost weights misclassified examples higher. Reduces both bias and variance.

3. Stacking. Train multiple base models, then a meta-learner on their out-of-fold predictions. Best when base models are diverse (e.g., tree + linear + NN).

4. XGBoost / LightGBM / CatBoost. Three optimized gradient-boosted tree libraries. XGBoost: most established. LightGBM: fastest on big data. CatBoost: best out-of-box for categoricals. All dominate tabular ML.

5. When to choose what. Bagging for variance problems. Boosting for max accuracy. Stacking when you have time and diverse base models. Tree ensembles dominate tabular — try these before deep learning.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Boosting too many trees without early stopping — classic overfit. Always pass eval_set + early_stopping_rounds.
  • Using default hyperparameters and assuming XGBoost is automatically better — without tuning, it often loses to a tuned RF.
  • Stacking with correlated base models — they make the same errors, so the ensemble does not help.

Quick recap

Bagging cuts variance via parallel resampling. Boosting cuts bias and variance sequentially. Stacking learns to combine diverse models. For tabular data, gradient boosting is the default first try.

Glossary

Bootstrap sample
Sampling with replacement from training data.
Out-of-fold prediction
Prediction made on a held-out fold during cross-validation.
Early stopping
Halting training when validation metric stops improving.
Weak learner
A model only slightly better than chance; building block for boosting.
"}, "D683/ch1/s3": {"title": "Advanced Regularization Techniques", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
Weight decayEquivalent to L2 regularization in optimizer settings.
Internal covariate shiftDistribution drift in layer activations during training; addressed by batch norm.
OverfittingModel performs much better on train than val/test.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — the modern regularization toolkit

WORKED EXAMPLE — regularizing a deep net that memorizes
Train acc 99%, val 74%. Stack the tools:
• Dropout 0.3 — random neurons silenced per batch → co-adaptation broken.
• Weight decay (L2/AdamW) — large weights taxed.
• Early stopping — halt at the validation-loss minimum.
• Data augmentation — flips/crops/noise multiply effective data (images); synonym swaps/back-translation (text).
• Batch normalization — stabilizes/regularizes as a side effect.
• Label smoothing — soften 1.0 targets to 0.9 so the net stops being overconfident.
After: train 92%, val 86%. Each tool trades a little bias for a lot of variance — tune ONE at a time.
⚠️ AUGMENT ONLY THE TRAINING SET
Augmenting validation/test data corrupts the measurement. And elastic net = L1 + L2 combined — the “which regularizer both selects features and shrinks?” answer.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Regularization controls overfitting without throwing away model capacity. Modern ML lives or dies by good regularization — every state-of-the-art deep network combines dropout, weight decay, and data augmentation.

Core concepts

1. L1, L2, ElasticNet. L1 (Lasso) shrinks coefficients toward zero, can produce sparsity. L2 (Ridge) shrinks all coefficients smoothly. ElasticNet combines both. Add penalty terms to your loss; strength is a hyperparameter.

2. Dropout. During training, randomly zero a fraction (0.2-0.5) of activations each forward pass. Forces the network to not rely on any single neuron. Standard for fully-connected layers.

3. Batch normalization. Normalize activations across the mini-batch, then learn an affine transform. Speeds training, reduces internal covariate shift, mild regularizing effect.

4. Early stopping. Track validation loss; stop when it stops improving for N epochs. Implicit regularization — you stop before the model memorizes training noise.

5. Data augmentation. Random transformations on training data (image flips, crops; text paraphrasing). Expands the training set effectively. For images, often beats architectural changes.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Stacking too many regularizers — at some point you starve the model of capacity. Add one at a time and measure.
  • Forgetting model.eval() at inference — dropout and batch norm behave differently in train vs eval mode.
  • Augmentation that destroys label-relevant info (e.g., flipping medical images where left/right matters).

Quick recap

Regularization techniques work together: weight penalties, structural (dropout, batch norm), training (early stopping), data (augmentation). Combine them to control overfitting while keeping model capacity.

Glossary

Weight decay
Equivalent to L2 regularization in optimizer settings.
Internal covariate shift
Distribution drift in layer activations during training; addressed by batch norm.
Overfitting
Model performs much better on train than val/test.
"}, "D683/ch1/s4": {"title": "Optimization Algorithms in Practice", "body": "
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — SGD to Adam, what each fix fixes

WORKED EXAMPLE — the optimizer upgrade path
• Batch GD: exact gradient on ALL data per step — too slow at scale.
• SGD (mini-batch): noisy gradient on 32-256 samples — cheap steps, noise even helps escape shallow minima.
• + Momentum: accumulate a velocity so zigzagging ravines straighten out.
• Adam: momentum + per-parameter adaptive learning rates — the robust default.
• + LR schedules: warmup then decay (cosine) — big steps early, fine steps late.
Reading curves: loss NaN/exploding → LR too high (or add gradient clipping); loss flat → LR too low or dead ReLUs; val loss rising while train falls → overfitting, stop.
⚠️ ADAM ≈ DEFAULT, NOT ALWAYS BEST
Well-tuned SGD+momentum sometimes generalizes better (vision); Adam(W) dominates transformers. The exam wants the trade-off sentence, not a religion.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Choosing the right optimizer can make a model train in 1 hour vs 10 — or fail to converge entirely. Adam is the default for good reason, but knowing when SGD with momentum wins matters for vision and other domains.

Core concepts

1. SGD and momentum. Stochastic Gradient Descent: update weights using gradient on a mini-batch. Momentum adds a velocity term that accelerates in consistent gradient directions. SGD+momentum is still SOTA for vision.

2. Adam and AdamW. Adam: adaptive learning rate per parameter using running estimates of gradient mean/variance. AdamW: Adam with decoupled weight decay. Default for transformers and most NLP.

3. Learning rate schedules. Decay LR over training: step decay, cosine, warmup-then-decay. Warmup is critical for transformers. Schedulers often matter more than the optimizer choice.

4. Vanishing and exploding gradients. Gradients shrink to zero or blow up over many layers. Mitigations: skip connections (ResNet), normalization layers, gradient clipping, careful initialization (Xavier, He).

5. Choosing optimizer per task. Vision/CNNs: SGD+momentum often wins. Transformers/NLP: AdamW. Tabular DL: Adam usually fine. Always tune learning rate first — it dominates other hyperparameters.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Forgetting LR warmup with transformers — training diverges in the first hundred steps.
  • Using Adam default LR (1e-3) for transformers — too high; 1e-4 to 5e-5 typical.
  • Not clipping gradients on RNNs — exploding gradients sink training silently.

Quick recap

Optimizers: SGD+momentum still rules vision; AdamW dominates NLP. Learning rate matters more than optimizer choice. Schedules and warmup are essential for stable training.

Glossary

Learning rate
Step size for parameter updates.
Momentum
Running average of past gradients to accelerate optimization.
Gradient clipping
Capping gradient norm to prevent explosions.

Step decay: a learning-rate schedule that reduces the LR at specified EPOCH BOUNDARIES — e.g., divide by 10 at epochs 30 and 60 — big steps early to explore, small steps late to settle.

"}, "D683/ch2/s1": {"title": "Feedforward Networks and Backpropagation", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
AutogradAutomatic differentiation; framework computes gradients automatically.
ActivationNon-linear function applied element-wise to layer output.
EpochOne full pass through training data.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — backpropagation on a two-layer net

WORKED EXAMPLE — forward, loss, backward, update
Input x=2 → hidden h = ReLU(0.5·2)=1 → output ŷ = 0.8·1 = 0.8; label y = 1; loss L = (ŷ−y)² = 0.04.
Backward (chain rule): dL/dŷ = 2(ŷ−y) = −0.4 → dL/dw₂ = −0.4·h = −0.4 → dL/dh = −0.4·0.8 = −0.32 → through ReLU (active, so pass) → dL/dw₁ = −0.32·x = −0.64.
Update (lr 0.1): w₂ = 0.8+0.04 = 0.84; w₁ = 0.5+0.064 = 0.564 → new ŷ ≈ 0.947 — closer to 1. ✓
That’s the whole engine: forward compute, measure loss, chain-rule the blame backward, nudge every weight. Deep nets do this across millions of weights per batch.
⚠️ VANISHING GRADIENTS EXPLAIN THE ARCHITECTURE ZOO
Multiplying many small derivatives → early layers learn nothing. ReLU (derivative 1), residual/skip connections, batch norm, and LSTM gates all exist to fight this — the “why” behind chapters ahead.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Every deep model — CNN, RNN, Transformer — is built on feedforward layers and trained with backpropagation. Understanding the forward and backward pass is the foundation for debugging anything that follows.

Core concepts

1. Forward pass. Each layer computes y = activation(Wx + b). Stack layers; input flows through. Final output goes into a loss function comparing it to the target.

2. Backward pass (backpropagation). Apply chain rule from loss back through the network to compute partial derivatives w.r.t. every weight. Modern frameworks (PyTorch, TF) compute this automatically via autograd.

3. Activation functions. Inject non-linearity. ReLU = max(0, x): default, fast. GELU/SwiGLU: smoother alternatives in transformers. Sigmoid/tanh: legacy, suffer from vanishing gradients.

4. Loss functions. Cross-entropy for classification. MSE/MAE for regression. Custom losses for ranking, detection, generation. The loss defines what 'good' means to the optimizer.

5. Universal approximation. A sufficiently wide single hidden layer can approximate any continuous function. In practice, depth is more efficient than width for representing complex functions.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Skipping the bias term — most layers need it for flexibility.
  • Using sigmoid in deep nets — vanishing gradients kill training. Use ReLU or GELU.
  • Forgetting to zero gradients each step (PyTorch: optimizer.zero_grad()) — gradients accumulate by default.

Quick recap

A feedforward net is alternating linear transforms and non-linear activations. Backprop computes gradients via chain rule. Choose activations and losses to match the task.

Glossary

Autograd
Automatic differentiation; framework computes gradients automatically.
Activation
Non-linear function applied element-wise to layer output.
Epoch
One full pass through training data.
"}, "D683/ch2/s2": {"title": "Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
Receptive fieldRegion of input that influences a given output activation.
Feature mapOutput of a convolutional filter.
Skip connectionDirect path that adds an earlier layer's output to a later layer (ResNet).
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — a convolution computed + a CNN’s shape

WORKED EXAMPLE — slide one 3×3 filter
A 3×3 edge filter over a 5×5 image patch: output pixel = Σ(filter × patch) — e.g. vertical-edge filter 10−110−110−1 on a bright-left/dark-right patch → large positive value = “edge here.” Slide it everywhere → a feature map. Output size: (5−3)/1+1 = 3×3 (stride 1, no padding).
A CNN stacks conv → ReLU → pooling (downsample) → conv … → dense classifier. Early layers learn edges; middle layers textures/parts; late layers objects. Weight sharing (one 3×3 filter = 9 weights scanned everywhere) is why CNNs need far fewer parameters than dense nets on images.
⚠️ CONVOLUTION = LOCAL + SHARED
Two exam words: locality (filters see small windows) and weight sharing (same filter everywhere → translation robustness). Output-size arithmetic ((W−F+2P)/S+1) is the standard computation question.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

CNNs revolutionized computer vision and remain the foundation of most production vision systems. Understanding their structure unlocks transfer learning and lets you adapt them for image, audio, and even tabular spatial data.

Core concepts

1. Convolution layer. A small filter (e.g., 3x3) slides across the input image, computing dot products. Each filter learns to detect a specific feature (edges, textures, then objects). Multiple filters per layer.

2. Pooling and stride. Pooling (max, average) downsamples spatial dimensions. Stride > 1 in convolution does the same. Reduces compute and grows receptive field.

3. Output dimensions. For input H×W with kernel k, padding p, stride s: output = (H + 2p − k) / s + 1. Knowing this avoids 'shape mismatch' errors mid-training.

4. Architectures. LeNet (1998): foundational. AlexNet (2012): GPU breakthrough. VGG: deeper. ResNet: skip connections enable >100 layers. EfficientNet: compound scaling. Vision Transformers now compete with CNNs.

5. Transfer learning. Take a CNN pretrained on ImageNet, replace the final classifier, fine-tune on your data. Typical small-dataset workflow. ResNet-50 and EfficientNet are strong defaults.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Forgetting to normalize input images the same way the pretrained model expects (ImageNet mean/std).
  • Training only the new final layer when you have enough data — often unfreezing the whole network does better.
  • Ignoring receptive field — small filters in shallow nets cannot see large objects.

Quick recap

CNNs use convolutions to learn spatial features hierarchically. Modern vision is built on transfer learning from pretrained CNNs (and increasingly Vision Transformers).

Glossary

Receptive field
Region of input that influences a given output activation.
Feature map
Output of a convolutional filter.
Skip connection
Direct path that adds an earlier layer's output to a later layer (ResNet).
"}, "D683/ch2/s3": {"title": "Recurrent Networks and LSTMs", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
Hidden stateRNN memory passed between time steps.
Cell stateLSTM's separate memory channel that flows mostly unchanged unless gates modify it.
GateSigmoid-activated multiplicative unit controlling info flow.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — an RNN step, and why LSTMs exist

WORKED EXAMPLE — carry a hidden state through “not good”
An RNN reads tokens one at a time, updating a hidden state h: h₁ = f(“not”, h₀); h₂ = f(“good”, h₁). The state carries “not”’s negation forward, so the sentiment head reads h₂ → negative. Same weights every step (recurrence).
On LONG sequences, repeated multiplication vanishes early information — the 100th step barely feels the 1st. LSTM/GRU add gates: forget (what to drop), input (what to store), output (what to expose) — a cell state that can carry information across hundreds of steps unchanged.
⚠️ SEQUENTIAL = SLOW
RNNs process token-by-token — no parallelism across the sequence, which (plus long-range limits) is exactly why transformers displaced them. That “why transformers won” contrast is the exam question.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

RNNs were the workhorse for sequence data (text, time series, audio) before Transformers. They still appear in production and on resource-constrained devices. Understanding their limitations also explains why Transformers won.

Core concepts

1. Vanilla RNN. Process sequence one element at a time, maintaining a hidden state h_t = f(W * x_t + U * h_{t-1}). Simple but suffers from vanishing gradients on long sequences.

2. LSTM. Long Short-Term Memory adds gates (input, forget, output) and a cell state. Gates learn what to remember and forget. Handles much longer sequences than vanilla RNN.

3. GRU. Gated Recurrent Unit: simpler than LSTM (2 gates vs 3), often comparable performance. Cheaper and faster to train.

4. Bidirectional RNNs. Run two RNNs — forward and backward — and concatenate outputs. Each position sees both past and future context. Used in NER, POS tagging.

5. When RNNs vs Transformers. RNNs: streaming inference, low memory, very long sequences (potentially). Transformers: parallelizable, much better quality on most NLP tasks. For new projects, default to Transformers.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Training RNNs without gradient clipping — exploding gradients break them silently.
  • Using vanilla RNN on long sequences — vanishing gradients mean the model effectively forgets early context.
  • Forgetting that RNNs cannot be parallelized over sequence length, making training slow.

Quick recap

RNNs process sequences step by step. LSTMs and GRUs add gating to handle long dependencies. Bidirectional variants see both directions. Mostly replaced by Transformers but still relevant for streaming.

Glossary

Hidden state
RNN memory passed between time steps.
Cell state
LSTM's separate memory channel that flows mostly unchanged unless gates modify it.
Gate
Sigmoid-activated multiplicative unit controlling info flow.
"}, "D683/ch2/s4": {"title": "Transformers and Attention", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
Causal maskTriangular mask preventing attention to future tokens.
Attention headOne independent attention computation; many run in parallel.
FlashAttentionMemory-efficient attention implementation; standard in modern systems.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — attention, computed in miniature

WORKED EXAMPLE — which word does “it” attend to?
“The cat drank the milk because it was thirsty.” For token “it”: its query vector dots against every token’s key vector → scores, softmaxed to weights: cat 0.62, milk 0.24, others crumbs → output = weighted sum of value vectors ≈ mostly “cat.” The model just resolved the pronoun — no recurrence, and every token attends to every other IN PARALLEL.
Multi-head = several attention patterns at once (syntax head, coreference head…). Positional encodings restore word order. Stack N of these blocks → BERT (encoder, understanding) / GPT (decoder, generation).
⚠️ Q·K CHOOSES, V CARRIES
Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QKᵀ/√d)V: queries match keys to decide WEIGHTS; values carry the content. Parallelism + long-range access = why transformers replaced RNNs — the two-sentence exam answer.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Transformers power GPT, BERT, T5, and every modern LLM. Self-attention is the single most important architectural innovation in deep learning since 2017. Understanding it is non-negotiable for AI engineering.

Core concepts

1. Self-attention. Each token attends to every other token, weighted by learned similarity. attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d)) V. Captures long-range dependencies in O(1) hops vs O(n) for RNNs.

2. Q, K, V. Three learned linear projections of input embeddings. Q = query (what am I looking for?), K = keys (what do I have?), V = values (what do I return?). Computed for every token.

3. Multi-head attention. Multiple independent attention heads run in parallel; each learns different patterns. Outputs concatenated and projected. Typical: 8-16 heads.

4. Encoder vs decoder vs encoder-decoder. Encoder-only (BERT): bidirectional, classification/embeddings. Decoder-only (GPT): autoregressive generation, causal mask. Encoder-decoder (T5): translation, summarization.

5. Position encoding. Self-attention is permutation-invariant — needs explicit position info. Sinusoidal (original), learned, RoPE (modern), ALiBi. Without it, the model cannot distinguish word order.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Forgetting the causal mask in decoder-only models — they would cheat by looking at future tokens during training.
  • O(n^2) attention memory — naive implementation OOMs on long sequences. Use FlashAttention or sliding window.
  • Not scaling by sqrt(d) — dot products grow with dimension, pushing softmax into saturation.

Quick recap

Transformers replaced RNNs by computing self-attention over all positions in parallel. Q/K/V projections, multi-head attention, and position encoding are the core building blocks.

Glossary

Causal mask
Triangular mask preventing attention to future tokens.
Attention head
One independent attention computation; many run in parallel.
FlashAttention
Memory-efficient attention implementation; standard in modern systems.
"}, "D683/ch2/s5": {"title": "Advanced Architectures: GANs, Autoencoders, Diffusion", "body": "
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — GANs, autoencoders, diffusion in one tour

WORKED EXAMPLE — three ways to generate a face
• GAN: a generator forges faces from noise; a discriminator judges real-vs-fake; they train adversarially until forgeries fool the judge. Sharp results; unstable training, mode collapse.
• Autoencoder: compress to a bottleneck (latent code), reconstruct out — learns structure; VAEs make the latent space smooth enough to SAMPLE new faces. Also great for anomaly detection (high reconstruction error = anomaly).
• Diffusion: start from pure noise, iteratively denoise step-by-step with a learned denoiser (trained by adding noise to real images and learning to undo it). Stable training, state-of-the-art quality — the engine of modern image generators.
Match by clue: adversarial pair → GAN; bottleneck/reconstruction → autoencoder; iterative denoising → diffusion.
⚠️ EACH HAS A SIGNATURE FAILURE
GAN → mode collapse/instability; autoencoder → blurry reconstructions; diffusion → slow sampling (many denoise steps). Symptom→architecture matching is the exam form.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Generative models create images, audio, text, and synthetic data. Each family has different strengths — GANs for sharp images, VAEs for structured latents, diffusion for state-of-the-art generation.

Core concepts

1. Autoencoders. Encoder compresses input to a latent vector; decoder reconstructs from it. Used for denoising, anomaly detection, dimensionality reduction. VAEs add a probabilistic latent.

2. GANs. Two networks: generator creates fakes, discriminator detects them. Trained adversarially. Famous for sharp images but hard to train (mode collapse, instability). StyleGAN is a milestone.

3. Diffusion models. Train a model to reverse a gradual noise-adding process. Generate by starting from noise and iteratively denoising. SOTA for images (Stable Diffusion, Imagen) and increasingly other modalities.

4. Comparing families. VAEs: structured latent, blurry outputs. GANs: sharp, hard to train. Diffusion: best quality, slow inference. Autoregressive: high quality, very slow generation.

5. Conditional generation. All families can be conditioned on text, class labels, or other modalities. Stable Diffusion conditions on text via CLIP embeddings + cross-attention.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • GAN mode collapse: generator outputs only a few unique samples. Use diverse architectures or different objectives (Wasserstein).
  • VAE blurriness from MSE reconstruction — use perceptual losses or hybrid VAE-GAN.
  • Diffusion inference is slow (50-1000 steps). Use distillation or DDIM/DPM-Solver for fewer steps.

Quick recap

Generative models trade off quality, sample speed, and training stability. Diffusion currently leads on image quality. Choose based on deployment constraints.

Glossary

Latent space
Learned compressed representation; meaningful directions can be navigated.
Mode collapse
Generator produces only a few outputs, ignoring data diversity.
Denoising step
One iteration of a diffusion model's reverse process.
"}, "D683/ch3/s1": {"title": "Text Preprocessing and Tokenization", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
OOVOut-of-vocabulary; word not in tokenizer vocab.
SubwordA token smaller than a word, often a morpheme.
Token IDInteger index into the embedding table.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.

📖 Worked example — preprocessing “unbelievable!” three ways

WORKED EXAMPLE — tokenization choices change everything
• Word-level: [“unbelievable”, “!”] — huge vocab, and “unbelieveable” (typo) = out-of-vocabulary.
• Character-level: [u,n,b,…] — tiny vocab, but sequences get long and meaning-poor.
• Subword (BPE/WordPiece — the modern default): [“un”, “believ”, “able”, “!”] — frequent chunks become tokens; ANY string decomposes, morphology is visible.
Classic pipeline extras: lowercase, stop-word removal, stemming (believ) vs lemmatization (believe) — used for bag-of-words/TF-IDF; modern transformer pipelines mostly just subword-tokenize and let the model learn the rest.
⚠️ SUBWORD KILLS OOV
“Why do modern models use BPE/WordPiece?” → no out-of-vocabulary failures + manageable vocab size + shared morphology. The three-part answer the exam wants.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Tokenization decisions cascade through every NLP pipeline. Choose poorly and your model cannot generalize, cannot handle multilingual text, or wastes context window on subword fragments.

Core concepts

1. Tokenization basics. Split text into discrete units the model consumes. Word-level: too sparse for OOV. Character-level: long sequences. Subword (BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece): the modern default.

2. BPE. Byte-Pair Encoding: start with characters, iteratively merge most frequent pairs into single tokens. GPT, LLaMA use BPE. Handles rare words by composing subwords.

3. WordPiece and SentencePiece. WordPiece (BERT): similar to BPE, picks merges that maximize likelihood. SentencePiece: language-agnostic, treats text as raw bytes — best for multilingual.

4. Special tokens. [CLS], [SEP], [PAD], [MASK] in BERT-style. , , in others. End-of-sequence and beginning-of-sequence tokens matter for generation.

5. Vocabulary trade-offs. Bigger vocab = fewer tokens per text but larger embedding table. 30k-100k typical. Multilingual models often 250k+. Token efficiency varies wildly across languages.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Tokenizing test data with a different tokenizer than training — guaranteed bad results.
  • Assuming tokens equal words — for English ~4 chars per token; for code or non-English, very different.
  • Forgetting to add special tokens that the pretrained model expects (e.g., [CLS] for classification).

Quick recap

Tokenization converts raw text into model-consumable IDs. BPE-family subword tokenizers dominate. Always use the tokenizer paired with your model.

Glossary

OOV
Out-of-vocabulary; word not in tokenizer vocab.
Subword
A token smaller than a word, often a morpheme.
Token ID
Integer index into the embedding table.

The [PAD] token fills shorter sequences in a batch so every sequence reaches equal length — tensors must be rectangular. Attention masks then tell the model to ignore the padding.

📊 FIGURE — models built for sequences
🎯 EXAM TIP
The defining property of a recurrent network is that it handles sequential data by carrying a hidden state across time steps. Everything that came after — LSTM, GRU, attention — is an answer to the same weakness: the plain RNN struggles to carry information across long distances.
"}, "D683/ch3/s2": {"body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
Cosine similarityStandard metric for embedding similarity; insensitive to magnitude.
MTEBMassive Text Embedding Benchmark; standard leaderboard.
RerankerCross-encoder that re-orders top-k retrieval candidates.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Embeddings convert text into dense vectors capturing semantic meaning. They power search, clustering, classification, and RAG. Picking the right embedding model is one of the highest-leverage decisions in an NLP system.

Core concepts

1. Word embeddings. Word2Vec, GloVe, FastText: each word gets one vector. Captures static semantic similarity (king - man + woman ≈ queen). Pre-2018 baseline.

2. Contextual embeddings. BERT, RoBERTa: same word gets different embeddings depending on context. Standard for modern NLP.

3. Sentence embeddings. sentence-transformers, OpenAI text-embedding-3, BGE: produce one vector per sentence. Used for similarity, clustering, retrieval. MTEB leaderboard ranks them.

4. Cross-encoders vs bi-encoders. Bi-encoder: encodes query and doc separately, fast retrieval via vector similarity. Cross-encoder: encodes them together, slower but more accurate.

5. Choosing embeddings. For retrieval: BGE, E5, OpenAI, Voyage. For multilingual: mE5, multilingual-MiniLM. For code: codeBERT or specialized code embeddings.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Mixing embeddings from different models — they live in different spaces, similarity is meaningless.
  • Using L2 distance when the model was trained for cosine similarity (or vice versa).
  • Treating embedding dim as more is better — bigger embeddings cost more, sometimes for marginal quality.

Quick recap

Embeddings turn text into vectors capturing semantic meaning. Static (Word2Vec) → contextual (BERT) → sentence-level. Pick a model trained for your task and language.

Glossary

Cosine similarity
Standard metric for embedding similarity; insensitive to magnitude.
MTEB
Massive Text Embedding Benchmark; standard leaderboard.
Reranker
Cross-encoder that re-orders top-k retrieval candidates.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — cosine similarity, computed by hand

Three tiny 3-dimensional embeddings. A = [3, 1, 0] is your query, B = [6, 2, 0] is a long document that says the same thing, and C = [0, 2, 3] is about something else.

1
Dot products: A·B = 3×6 + 1×2 + 0×0 = 20 and A·C = 3×0 + 1×2 + 0×3 = 2.
2
Norms: |A| = √(9+1+0) = 3.162, |B| = √(36+4+0) = 6.325, |C| = √(0+4+9) = 3.606.
3
Cosine: cos(A,B) = 20 / (3.162 × 6.325) = 1.000 and cos(A,C) = 2 / (3.162 × 3.606) = 0.175.
4
Now L2 distance instead: ||A-B|| = √(9+1+0) = 3.162 and ||A-C|| = √(9+1+9) = 4.359.

Output: cos(A,B) = 1.000, cos(A,C) = 0.175 — L2(A,B) = 3.162, L2(A,C) = 4.359

B is exactly 2 × A, so it points in the identical direction and cosine scores it a perfect 1.00 — length does not matter. But L2 still puts B 3.16 units away, purely because it is longer. That is the whole reason embedding models trained with a cosine objective must be scored with cosine: a wordy document and a short one that mean the same thing differ in magnitude, and only cosine ignores that. The trap is switching metrics between indexing and querying.

Figure — why both encoders exist: the bi-encoder is the only one cheap enough to touch every document, the cross-encoder is the only one accurate enough to order the finalists

"}, "D683/ch3/s3": {"title": "Language Models and Pretraining", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
PretrainingSelf-supervised training on large unlabeled text.
Fine-tuningContinued training on a specific downstream task.
LoRALow-Rank Adaptation; parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — pretrain once, fine-tune everywhere

WORKED EXAMPLE — from raw text to a ticket classifier
1. Pretrain (done by the lab): predict masked words (BERT) or next tokens (GPT) over billions of words — the model learns grammar, facts, style. Self-supervised: the text labels itself.
2. Fine-tune (done by you): add a classification head, train on 5,000 labeled tickets for a few epochs → 90%+ where from-scratch would flounder.
3. Cheaper adaptations: frozen features (train only the head), LoRA/adapters (tiny trainable inserts), or prompting/in-context learning (no training at all).
Scaling laws: more data + parameters + compute → predictably lower loss — why models keep growing.
⚠️ MASKED vs CAUSAL
BERT-style = masked LM, bidirectional, best for UNDERSTANDING tasks. GPT-style = causal next-token, unidirectional, best for GENERATION. Matching objective→architecture→use is the exam’s repeated triple.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Modern NLP is built on pretrained language models. Understanding the pretraining objectives explains why BERT works for classification, GPT for generation, and T5 for both.

Core concepts

1. Causal LM (GPT). Predict next token given previous ones. Trained left-to-right with causal mask. Natural fit for generation. GPT family, LLaMA, Mistral.

2. Masked LM (BERT). Mask 15% of tokens randomly, predict them from bidirectional context. Strong for classification, NER, QA. BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa.

3. Encoder-decoder (T5, BART). Encoder reads input; decoder generates output. Pretrained on span corruption. Best for translation, summarization, sequence-to-sequence tasks.

4. Pretraining at scale. Train on billions of tokens of web text. Compute often dominates everything else. Chinchilla scaling laws: more data, smaller models often win.

5. Fine-tuning vs prompting. Fine-tuning: continue training on your task data. Prompting: use the model zero/few-shot. Prompting often wins for limited data; fine-tuning when you have lots and need consistency.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Fine-tuning a giant model on a small dataset — overfitting and catastrophic forgetting. Use LoRA / PEFT.
  • Using BERT for generation — it cannot, the architecture is wrong. Use T5 or GPT-style.
  • Ignoring tokenizer when fine-tuning — using a different tokenizer than pretraining destroys the embeddings.

Quick recap

Pretrained LMs come in three flavors based on objective: causal (GPT), masked (BERT), encoder-decoder (T5). Match objective to task.

Glossary

Pretraining
Self-supervised training on large unlabeled text.
Fine-tuning
Continued training on a specific downstream task.
LoRA
Low-Rank Adaptation; parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
"}, "D683/ch3/s4": {"title": "NLP Tasks: Classification, NER, QA", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
BIO taggingBegin/Inside/Outside scheme for sequence labeling.
SpanContiguous tokens; how extractive QA returns answers.
PipelineHuggingFace's high-level inference API.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — one review through three NLP tasks

WORKED EXAMPLE — “Anna Smith loved the Berlin hotel, but checkout was slow.”
• Classification (sentiment): overall mixed-positive — one label for the sequence.
• NER: [Anna Smith → PERSON], [Berlin → LOC] — a label per TOKEN (sequence labeling).
• QA: “What was slow?” → span extraction: “checkout”.
Each task = same pretrained encoder + a different head: sequence-level softmax, per-token softmax, span start/end pointers. Metrics differ too: accuracy/F1, entity-level F1, exact-match/F1 — and summarization/translation add ROUGE/BLEU.
⚠️ TASK TYPE = OUTPUT SHAPE
One label → classification. Label per token → NER/tagging. Text span → extractive QA. Generated text → summarization/translation. Identify the output shape and the task (and metric) follows.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Most NLP work is one of a handful of tasks. Knowing which architecture and dataset shape fits each task is how you ship NLP features quickly.

Core concepts

1. Text classification. Predict a label for a document. Sentiment, spam, topic, intent. BERT-style encoder + classification head, or zero-shot via LLM.

2. Named entity recognition. Tag each token with an entity type (PERSON, LOCATION, ORG). Token-level classification. BIO or BIOES tagging schemes. spaCy is great for production NER.

3. Question answering. Extractive QA: find answer span in a passage. Generative QA: produce free-form answer. SQuAD-style benchmarks. Modern systems use RAG.

4. Summarization. Extractive: pick key sentences. Abstractive: generate new text. Encoder-decoder models (T5, BART, PEGASUS) excel. ROUGE for evaluation but human review remains essential.

5. Evaluation. Accuracy/F1 for classification. Token F1 / span match for NER. Exact match + F1 for extractive QA. ROUGE/BLEU for generation but they are imperfect.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Using accuracy for imbalanced classification — 99% accuracy means nothing if the positive class is 1%.
  • Token-level metrics for NER without entity-level evaluation — misses entity boundaries.
  • Trusting BLEU/ROUGE alone for generation — models can game them; spot-check outputs.

Quick recap

Classification, NER, QA, and summarization are the bread-and-butter NLP tasks. Each maps to a model architecture and evaluation metric.

Glossary

BIO tagging
Begin/Inside/Outside scheme for sequence labeling.
Span
Contiguous tokens; how extractive QA returns answers.
Pipeline
HuggingFace's high-level inference API.
"}, "D683/ch4/s1": {"title": "Image Classification at Scale", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
BackboneFeature-extracting body of a vision model, before the task-specific head.
Top-k accuracyWhether the true label is in the top-k predictions.
MixupAugmentation that linearly interpolates pairs of images and labels.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — training image classification at scale

WORKED EXAMPLE — the modern recipe on 100k product photos
1. Don’t start from scratch: take a ResNet/ViT pretrained on ImageNet; replace the head; fine-tune.
2. Augment: crops, flips, color jitter — effective dataset ×10.
3. Batch + schedule: mini-batches on GPU, warmup + cosine decay, mixed precision for speed.
4. Residual connections are why 50+ layer nets train at all (gradients skip through).
5. Evaluate honestly: top-1/top-5 accuracy, confusion matrix per class — the 2% overall error hiding 30% error on one rare class is the finding that matters.
Result: 94% top-1 in hours, vs weeks-and-worse from scratch.
⚠️ RESNET’S TRICK IS THE EXAM FACT
Skip connections let layers learn RESIDUALS (adjustments), keeping gradients alive in very deep nets — the one-sentence answer to “why did ResNets enable depth?”
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Image classification is the foundation of computer vision and the playground where most architectures (CNNs, ViTs) prove themselves. Almost every production vision system starts here.

Core concepts

1. ImageNet and transfer learning. ImageNet (1.4M images, 1000 classes) is the standard pretraining dataset. Almost all production models start from ImageNet weights and fine-tune.

2. Backbone architectures. ResNet (skip connections), EfficientNet (compound scaling), Vision Transformers (ViT, Swin). ResNet-50 is the safe default; EfficientNet-B0 to B7 for quality/speed trade-offs.

3. Data augmentation. Random crops, flips, color jitter, RandAugment, Mixup, CutMix. Often the single largest win in vision — easily +2-5% accuracy.

4. Class imbalance. Real-world classes are skewed. Solutions: weighted loss, focal loss, oversampling. Always check per-class metrics, not just overall accuracy.

5. Evaluation metrics. Top-1 / top-5 accuracy for many classes. Per-class precision/recall/F1 for imbalanced. Confusion matrix to spot systematic errors.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Forgetting to normalize input images with ImageNet mean/std — model sees garbage.
  • Tiny dataset + huge model = overfit. Use stronger augmentation, smaller model, or freeze backbone.
  • Single-number metrics hiding minority-class disasters. Always look at confusion matrices.

Quick recap

Image classification: pick a strong backbone, pretrain or transfer, augment aggressively, balance classes. Per-class metrics beat overall accuracy.

Glossary

Backbone
Feature-extracting body of a vision model, before the task-specific head.
Top-k accuracy
Whether the true label is in the top-k predictions.
Mixup
Augmentation that linearly interpolates pairs of images and labels.
"}, "D683/ch4/s2": {"title": "Object Detection and Segmentation", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
NMSNon-maximum suppression: removes overlapping detections of same object.
FPNFeature Pyramid Network: multi-scale features for detecting objects at different sizes.
SAMSegment Anything Model; zero-shot promptable segmentation by Meta.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — detection & segmentation, IoU computed

WORKED EXAMPLE — grade a predicted box
Ground-truth box area 100; predicted box overlaps 60 of it; union area 140. IoU = 60/140 ≈ 0.43 — below the usual 0.5 threshold → counted as a miss. mAP averages precision over classes/thresholds — detection’s headline metric.
The ladder: classification (whole image) → detection (boxes: two-stage Faster R-CNN = propose-then-classify, accurate; one-stage YOLO/SSD = single pass, fast) → semantic segmentation (label every pixel) → instance segmentation (Mask R-CNN: separate masks per object).
Choose by need: count cars → detection; measure tumor area → segmentation; real-time video → one-stage.
⚠️ SEMANTIC vs INSTANCE
Semantic: all cars share one “car” mask. Instance: car #1 vs car #2 separated. The distinction (and IoU arithmetic) are the two testable items.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Detection and segmentation are where vision becomes useful in industry: counting items, finding defects, autonomous driving, medical imaging. The architectures differ from classification — you need to localize, not just label.

Core concepts

1. Object detection. Predict bounding boxes + class labels. Two-stage (Faster R-CNN): propose regions, then classify. One-stage (YOLO, SSD): single forward pass, faster. DETR uses transformers.

2. Semantic vs instance segmentation. Semantic: pixel-level class labels (no instance separation). Instance: separate pixel masks per object. Mask R-CNN is the standard for instance segmentation.

3. IoU and mAP. Intersection over Union: predicted box ∩ true box / union. Threshold (0.5 typical) decides if a detection counts. Mean Average Precision averages across IoU thresholds and classes.

4. Anchors and anchor-free detectors. Older detectors use predefined box shapes (anchors) at each location. Newer (FCOS, DETR) directly predict boxes — simpler but sometimes harder to train.

5. Choosing per task. Real-time / edge: YOLO, EfficientDet. Best accuracy: DETR variants. Pixel masks needed: Mask R-CNN, Mask2Former. Foundation models: Segment Anything (SAM).

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Forgetting NMS (non-maximum suppression) post-processing — same object detected multiple times.
  • Tiny objects: standard detectors miss them. Use multi-scale training, FPN backbones.
  • Class imbalance in dense detectors — use focal loss (RetinaNet) or sample mining.

Quick recap

Object detection localizes and classifies. Segmentation produces pixel masks. IoU and mAP are the standard metrics. Modern transformer-based detectors and foundation models (SAM) are reshaping this space.

Glossary

NMS
Non-maximum suppression: removes overlapping detections of same object.
FPN
Feature Pyramid Network: multi-scale features for detecting objects at different sizes.
SAM
Segment Anything Model; zero-shot promptable segmentation by Meta.
"}, "D683/ch4/s3": {"title": "Multimodal Models (CLIP, Vision-Language Models)", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
Contrastive learningTraining objective that pulls matching pairs together and pushes non-matches apart.
Zero-shotPerforming a task without task-specific training data.
VLMVision-Language Model; takes images + text, outputs text.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — how CLIP connects pictures to words

WORKED EXAMPLE — zero-shot classification with no training
CLIP trained on 400M (image, caption) pairs with a contrastive objective: matching pairs pulled together in a shared embedding space, mismatches pushed apart.
To classify a photo with NO task-specific training: embed the image; embed the texts “a photo of a cat”, “a photo of a dog”, “a photo of a truck”; cosine-compare → highest similarity wins → zero-shot classification. New classes = new text prompts, zero retraining.
The same shared space powers text→image search, image captioning pipelines, and vision-language models (LLaVA-style: vision encoder feeding an LLM) that answer questions ABOUT images.
⚠️ CONTRASTIVE = PULL/PUSH
“How did CLIP learn without labels?” → natural captions as supervision, contrastive pull-matching/push-mismatching. “Why zero-shot?” → classification becomes nearest-text-embedding. Two answers, one space.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Multimodal models bridge text and images, enabling zero-shot classification, visual search, and image captioning. CLIP changed what is possible — and modern VLMs (GPT-4V, Claude with vision) extend it dramatically.

Core concepts

1. CLIP. Trained contrastively on 400M image-text pairs. Image encoder + text encoder produce vectors in shared space. Similar images and matching captions are nearby. Enables zero-shot classification.

2. Zero-shot classification. Score each candidate label by encoding 'a photo of a [label]' as text and the image, computing similarity. No labeled training data needed for the new task.

3. Vision-language models. GPT-4V, Claude 3 vision, LLaVA, Qwen-VL. Take images alongside text, generate text. Use visual encoders + projection into LLM context. Powerful and rapidly improving.

4. Image generation conditioning. Stable Diffusion uses CLIP text embeddings to condition image generation. The text encoder is the bridge between language and pixels.

5. Use cases. Visual search, content moderation, accessibility (image captioning), document understanding, robotic perception, medical image analysis.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • CLIP trained on web data has biases (overrepresented Western culture). Audit before deployment.
  • Treating VLMs as flawless — they hallucinate just like text-only LLMs, sometimes more.
  • Resolution loss: most VLMs downsample images significantly. Fine details often lost.

Quick recap

Multimodal models like CLIP unify vision and language in a shared embedding space. VLMs extend this for free-form text generation conditioned on images.

Glossary

Contrastive learning
Training objective that pulls matching pairs together and pushes non-matches apart.
Zero-shot
Performing a task without task-specific training data.
VLM
Vision-Language Model; takes images + text, outputs text.
"}, "D683/ch5/s1": {"title": "From Notebook to Production", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
SerializationSaving a model to a file for later loading.
ContainerLightweight isolated runtime environment (Docker).
ArtifactAny output of an ML run (model, metrics, config).
Version your training datayou may need to reproduce or audit a model later, and the exact data that trained it is half the recipe.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — notebook to production, the checklist

WORKED EXAMPLE — what changes when the model leaves Jupyter
The 0.89-F1 notebook model must become a service:
1. Refactor: notebook cells → a package (train.py, predict.py, features.py) with tests; pin dependencies.
2. Version everything: code (git), data (DVC/snapshots), model artifacts (registry) — reproducibility = same three inputs, same model.
3. Pipeline: ingest → validate → features → train → evaluate → register, automated (Airflow/Kubeflow) — not hand-run cells.
4. The feature-skew guard: the SAME feature code serves training and inference.
5. CI for ML: on every change, run tests + train on a sample + compare metrics against the current champion before promotion.
MLOps = DevOps + data/model versioning + continuous evaluation.
⚠️ REPRODUCIBILITY IS THE FIRST GATE
“Can anyone retrain this exact model?” If code/data/params aren’t versioned together, the answer is no — and that’s the first thing MLOps questions probe.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Most ML models never reach production. The gap between a Jupyter notebook and a reliable production service is where real engineering happens — and where most projects die.

Core concepts

1. Notebook to module. Refactor exploration code into clean .py modules. Functions and classes; tests; type hints; documented inputs/outputs. Notebook is where you discover; modules are where you ship.

2. Model serialization. Save model weights and metadata together: pickle/joblib for sklearn, state_dict for PyTorch, SavedModel for TF. Version your serialization format.

3. Containerization. Docker: package model + dependencies + runtime into a portable image. Same image runs locally, in CI, and in production. Multi-stage builds keep images small.

4. Batch vs real-time. Batch: predictions periodically (overnight scoring). Real-time: per-request inference (chatbots, recommendations). Different infrastructure: batch is cheaper, real-time more complex.

5. Artifact tracking. MLflow, Weights & Biases, DVC: track which code, data, hyperparameters produced which model. Reproducibility is non-negotiable in production.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Pickled models breaking after a library upgrade — pin dependencies, save model with versions.
  • Forgetting to set the model in eval mode in PyTorch — dropout still active during inference.
  • Building a real-time service when batch would suffice — overengineering wastes effort.

Quick recap

Production ML is engineering, not science. Refactor, containerize, version artifacts, choose batch vs real-time deliberately. Reproducibility comes from tracking code + data + hyperparameters together.

Glossary

Serialization
Saving a model to a file for later loading.
Container
Lightweight isolated runtime environment (Docker).
Artifact
Any output of an ML run (model, metrics, config).

Version your training data — you may need to reproduce or audit a model later, and the exact data that trained it is half the recipe. ONNX is the cross-framework model format: train in one framework, run in another.

"}, "D683/ch5/s2": {"title": "Serving Models: APIs, vLLM, TorchServe", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
ThroughputRequests served per second.
LatencyTime per request, end to end.
KV cacheStored key/value attention states to skip recomputation in autoregressive generation.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — choosing a serving strategy

WORKED EXAMPLE — four workloads, four setups
• Fraud check inside a payment flow (10ms budget) → real-time API (FastAPI/TorchServe container), autoscaled replicas behind a load balancer.
• Nightly churn scores for 2M customers → batch job — throughput over latency.
• Chat assistant on an LLM → GPU serving with vLLM: continuous batching + KV-cache paging squeeze many concurrent generations per GPU; token streaming for UX.
• Mobile offline feature → edge: quantized (int8) distilled model on-device.
Cross-cutting tools: quantization/distillation shrink models; A/B or shadow deployment gates rollouts; autoscaling meets traffic.
⚠️ LLM SERVING ≠ CLASSIFIER SERVING
Generation is stateful (KV cache) and token-by-token — hence specialized servers (vLLM) and metrics like time-to-first-token. Applying classifier-serving logic to LLMs is the modern trap question.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

An ML model in a file is not a product. Serving is how it becomes one — and the difference between 100ms and 5s response time can make or break user experience.

Core concepts

1. FastAPI for inference. Async Python web framework. Wrap your model in a POST /predict endpoint. Pydantic for input validation. Uvicorn for production. Standard stack for ML APIs.

2. vLLM and TGI for LLMs. Specialized servers for LLM inference. PagedAttention KV cache, continuous batching, optimized kernels. Order of magnitude faster than naive transformers serving.

3. TorchServe and TF Serving. Production-grade servers for PyTorch and TensorFlow models. Versioning, metrics, batching, multi-model serving. Heavier setup but more features than rolling your own.

4. Batching and throughput. Batch multiple requests together for GPU efficiency. Trade latency for throughput. Continuous batching (vLLM) does this dynamically.

5. Async patterns. Use async/await for I/O-bound work (fetching context, calling external APIs). Keeps request handlers from blocking each other.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Synchronous Python web servers + ML — one slow request blocks all others. Use async or workers.
  • Naive batching that waits forever for a full batch — bound batch wait time to keep latency in check.
  • Forgetting to warm up the model at startup — first request is 10x slower than the rest.

Quick recap

Choose your serving tech based on the model: FastAPI for general; vLLM/TGI for LLMs; TorchServe/TF Serving for heavyweight production. Batch for throughput, async for concurrency.

Glossary

Throughput
Requests served per second.
Latency
Time per request, end to end.
KV cache
Stored key/value attention states to skip recomputation in autoregressive generation.

INT8 quantization typically reduces model size and speeds inference with a slight accuracy cost — the standard deployment trade. vLLM exposes an OpenAI-compatible API, letting you drop-in replace OpenAI client calls with a self-hosted server. For edge/on-device inference, prefer quantized small models exported to ONNX, CoreML, or TFLite.

"}, "D683/ch5/s3": {"title": "Monitoring and Drift Detection", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
PSIPopulation Stability Index; measures distribution drift between datasets.
KS testKolmogorov-Smirnov; tests whether two samples come from the same distribution.
Ground truthActual correct label, often only available with delay.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.
📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — catching drift with numbers

WORKED EXAMPLE — three drifts, three detections
• Data drift: input distribution moves — avg transaction amount jumps 40% after a pricing change. Detect: PSI/KS tests per feature against the training distribution.
• Prediction drift: output rate moves — fraud flags 2% → 9% overnight. Detect: monitor score distributions.
• Concept drift: the X→y mapping itself changes — fraudsters adapt; live F1 (once labels arrive) slides 0.85 → 0.68. Detect: delayed-label performance tracking.
Response ladder: alert → diagnose (which features moved?) → retrain on recent data → A/B the challenger. Retraining cadence: scheduled (monthly) or triggered (drift threshold breached).
⚠️ DATA DRIFT CAN PRECEDE PERFORMANCE DROP
Input drift is the smoke alarm — it fires BEFORE labels arrive to prove damage. Monitoring only accuracy (which lags by label delay) misses the early warning; that timing insight is the exam question.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Models degrade silently. A model that was 95% accurate at deployment can quietly drop to 70% as the world changes — and you would not notice without monitoring. Drift detection is the early warning system.

Core concepts

1. Data drift. P(X) changes — input distribution shifts. Example: customer demographics evolve, sensor readings drift. Detected via statistical tests (KS, PSI) on input features.

2. Concept drift. P(y|X) changes — the relationship between inputs and labels shifts. Harder to detect; requires labels to fully diagnose.

3. Performance monitoring. Track accuracy, F1, AUC over time. Compute on labeled samples (delayed) and proxies (confidence distributions, prediction distribution).

4. Operational metrics. Latency p50/p95/p99, error rates, throughput, resource utilization. These show problems before quality degrades.

5. Retraining triggers. Schedule-based (weekly), drift-based (PSI > threshold), performance-based (accuracy drops). Document the policy and automate it.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Monitoring only operational metrics — misses model quality decay.
  • Setting drift thresholds too tight — constant false alarms cause alert fatigue.
  • Retraining without ground-truth labels — you need to actually verify the new model is better.

Quick recap

Monitor data drift, concept drift, performance, and operational metrics together. Define retraining triggers and automate them. Catch decay before users do.

Glossary

PSI
Population Stability Index; measures distribution drift between datasets.
KS test
Kolmogorov-Smirnov; tests whether two samples come from the same distribution.
Ground truth
Actual correct label, often only available with delay.

Monitoring stack: Datadog and Grafana are the standard dashboards/alerting tools. Production logs should NOT contain everything — exclude secrets/PII and drown-out noise; log what you would need at 3am. Alert on metrics that demand action (error rate, latency, drift), not vanity numbers. Champion/challenger: the champion is the currently-deployed model; challengers are candidates evaluated against it before promotion.

"}, "D683/ch5/s4": {"title": "A/B Testing and Experimentation", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
A/B testRandomized comparison between two variants in production.
Statistical powerProbability of detecting a true effect when one exists.
CanaryGradual rollout to detect issues before full deployment.
Proxy-vs-goal trapoptimizing click-through rate while harming retention is the classic case — the metric rose while the mission fell.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.

📖 Worked example — an A/B test on a model, done right

WORKED EXAMPLE — champion vs challenger recommender
1. Hypothesis + metric FIRST: challenger lifts click-through ≥ 0.5 points; guardrails: latency, revenue not degraded.
2. Randomize users (not requests — one user must see one variant) 50/50.
3. Power the test: compute needed sample size; run the full planned duration.
4. Result: champion 10.1% CTR, challenger 10.9%, p < 0.01 → significant lift → promote gradually (10% → 50% → 100%).
Safer variants: shadow mode (challenger predicts silently, compared offline) and canary (5% of traffic) before the full A/B. The cardinal sin: peeking daily and stopping at the first significant blip — inflates false positives.
⚠️ OFFLINE WIN ≠ ONLINE WIN
Better validation F1 doesn’t guarantee better business metrics (feedback loops, UX effects) — which is WHY live experiments exist. That justification is the graded answer.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Better offline metrics do not always mean better online performance. A/B testing models in production is how you know if your change actually helps users.

Core concepts

1. A/B test design. Randomly assign users to control (current model) and treatment (new model). Measure the metric you care about over a fixed window. Compute statistical significance.

2. Sample size and power. Larger expected effect = smaller sample needed. Use a power calculator before launching. Stopping early because results look good = false positives.

3. Shadow mode. New model runs on production traffic but its predictions are not served — only logged. Lets you validate quality and latency without user-facing risk.

4. Canary deployment. Roll out to 1% of traffic, then 5%, 25%, 100%. Watch metrics at each stage; auto-rollback if regression. Standard for risky launches.

5. Statistical significance. p-value < 0.05 typical. But also consider effect size — a tiny but significant improvement might not be worth deployment risk.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Looking at the test daily and stopping when you see significance — peeking inflates false positive rate.
  • Running too many simultaneous tests without correction — multiple comparisons.
  • Ignoring novelty effects — users react to anything new initially; let the test run long enough.

Quick recap

A/B testing is how production ML proves itself. Pre-register your metric, calculate sample size, do not peek. Use shadow mode and canaries to de-risk launches.

Glossary

A/B test
Randomized comparison between two variants in production.
Statistical power
Probability of detecting a true effect when one exists.
Canary
Gradual rollout to detect issues before full deployment.

Proxy-vs-goal trap: optimizing click-through rate while harming retention is the classic case — the metric rose while the mission fell. SUTVA and social networks: A/B tests can be contaminated because treated users’ behavior affects their untreated friends — spillover breaks the independence assumption.

📊 FIGURE — bandit testing against a fixed A/B split
🎯 EXAM TIP
A multi-armed bandit adapts the traffic allocation toward winning arms while the experiment runs, balancing exploration against exploitation. That earns more conversions during the test than a fixed A/B split, at the cost of cleaner statistics at the end.
"}, "D683/ch6/s1": {"title": "Bias and Fairness in ML", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
Disparate impactDifferent outcome rates across protected groups.
Demographic parityEqual positive prediction rate across groups.
CalibrationPredicted probability matches observed frequency.
Bias has three doorsit enters through the DATA (skewed samples, label errors), the FEATURES (proxies for protected attributes), and the OPTIMIZATION choices (what the objective rewards).
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.

📖 Worked example — a fairness audit with actual numbers

WORKED EXAMPLE — the lending model, audited by group
Disaggregate metrics: Group A — approval 40%, TPR 80%; Group B — approval 28%, TPR 65%. The overall accuracy (91%) hid a 15-point TPR gap.
Name the criteria (they CONFLICT, pick consciously):
• Demographic parity: equal approval rates.
• Equal opportunity: equal TPR among qualified applicants (often the lending choice).
• Equalized odds: equal TPR and FPR.
Mitigate: pre- (rebalance/remove proxies) / in- (fairness constraints) / post-processing (per-group thresholds) — then re-audit and monitor continuously. Impossibility result: you generally cannot satisfy all criteria at once; document the chosen trade-off.
⚠️ REMOVING THE SENSITIVE COLUMN ISN’T ENOUGH
Proxies (ZIP, names, purchase patterns) reconstruct it — “fairness through unawareness” fails. Auditing OUTCOMES by group is the required practice and the exam answer.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

An ML system that performs differently across demographic groups can do real harm — denying loans, misdiagnosing patients, over-policing communities. Detecting and mitigating bias is both an ethical and legal responsibility.

Core concepts

1. Sources of bias. Historical bias in training data, sampling bias (under-represented groups), labeling bias (annotators' assumptions), feedback loops (predictions changing future data).

2. Fairness metrics. Demographic parity (equal positive rate across groups). Equal opportunity (equal TPR). Equalized odds (equal TPR and FPR). Calibration (predicted prob equals true prob across groups). Often mutually exclusive.

3. Pre-, in-, and post-processing mitigation. Pre: rebalance data, remove biased features. In-process: fairness-aware loss. Post: adjust decision thresholds per group. Each has trade-offs.

4. Auditing in production. Monitor metrics broken down by demographic group. Disparate impact ratios (4/5ths rule heuristic). Document audits in model cards.

5. Limits of mitigation. You cannot satisfy all fairness criteria simultaneously (Chouldechova). Choose explicitly. Engineering decisions are also social decisions.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Removing the protected attribute (race, gender) and assuming bias is gone — proxies (zip code, name) leak it back.
  • Only checking aggregate accuracy — group disparities hide inside.
  • Treating fairness as a one-time audit — distributions change, biases re-emerge.

Quick recap

Bias enters at every stage. Audit per-group, choose fairness criteria explicitly, mitigate at the right stage, and monitor continuously. Document in model cards.

Glossary

Disparate impact
Different outcome rates across protected groups.
Demographic parity
Equal positive prediction rate across groups.
Calibration
Predicted probability matches observed frequency.

Bias has three doors: it enters through the DATA (skewed samples, label errors), the FEATURES (proxies for protected attributes), and the OPTIMIZATION choices (what the objective rewards). Auditing means checking all three.

📊 FIGURE — fairness is a values decision, not a metric choice
🎯 EXAM TIP
Fairness decisions should involve affected stakeholders, ethicists and domain experts, not only the modelling team. The technical reason is concrete: the common fairness definitions are mathematically incompatible, so you cannot satisfy them all — choosing which to optimise is a values judgement.
"}, "D683/ch6/s2": {"title": "Privacy: Differential Privacy and Federated Learning", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
EpsilonPrivacy budget in DP — smaller is more private but costs accuracy.
Federated learningDistributed training where data stays on client devices.
Linkage attackRe-identification by combining anonymized data with auxiliary info.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.

📖 Worked example — differential privacy & federated learning, concretely

WORKED EXAMPLE — two privacy technologies at work
Differential privacy: a hospital publishes disease statistics with calibrated noise. Query “how many patients have X?” → true 143 → released 145. The ε (epsilon) budget bounds how much any ONE patient’s presence can shift outputs — remove any individual and answers look statistically identical, so membership can’t be inferred. DP-SGD applies the same idea to model training (clipped, noised gradients).

Federated learning: phones improve a keyboard model WITHOUT uploading keystrokes — each device trains locally, sends only weight UPDATES; the server averages them (FedAvg). Data never leaves the device; combine with secure aggregation + DP because raw updates can still leak.
⚠️ EPSILON IS THE PRIVACY DIAL
Smaller ε = stronger privacy = noisier answers/less accuracy. And federated ≠ automatically private — updates leak without DP/secure aggregation. Both caveats are exam material.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

ML on sensitive data (health, finance, personal communications) needs privacy guarantees beyond access controls. Differential privacy and federated learning give mathematical and architectural protection respectively.

Core concepts

1. Differential privacy (DP). A mechanism is ε-DP if its output distribution barely changes when one record is added or removed. Provides a formal privacy budget. Implemented by adding calibrated noise.

2. DP-SGD. Differentially private stochastic gradient descent. Clip per-example gradients, add Gaussian noise. Trains models with DP guarantees but with some accuracy cost.

3. Federated learning. Train across many devices/organizations without centralizing data. Each client computes a local update; server aggregates. Used by Apple keyboards, hospital networks.

4. Secure aggregation. Federated updates can still leak info. Secure aggregation (cryptographic) ensures the server only sees the sum, not individual contributions.

5. PII and ML pipelines. Strip identifiers before training, log carefully, audit for memorization. LLMs can memorize training data; query them to test.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Assuming anonymization is enough — it can be reversed via linkage attacks. DP is the formal answer.
  • DP with too small an epsilon — destroys utility. Larger epsilon may be acceptable depending on sensitivity.
  • Federated learning without secure aggregation — server sees individual updates, partial leak.

Quick recap

Privacy needs more than access control. Differential privacy provides formal guarantees with a budget. Federated learning keeps data on-device. Combine techniques and audit.

Glossary

Epsilon
Privacy budget in DP — smaller is more private but costs accuracy.
Federated learning
Distributed training where data stays on client devices.
Linkage attack
Re-identification by combining anonymized data with auxiliary info.

PII detection tooling: Microsoft Presidio is the standard open-source tool for detecting and redacting personally identifiable information in text — names, phones, SSNs — before data enters training or logs.

📊 FIGURE — what the regulation asks of an ML system
🎯 EXAM TIP
GDPR can require data subject rights, potentially including a right to explanation for automated decisions — Article 22 is the provision usually cited. In practice this is what pushes a team toward an interpretable model, or toward being able to explain a black-box one.
"}, "D683/ch6/s3": {"title": "Explainability and Transparency", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
SHAPSHapley Additive exPlanations; per-feature contribution to a prediction.
Model cardStructured doc describing model intent, performance, and limits.
CounterfactualWhat would change the model's decision; useful for explanation.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.

📖 Worked example — explaining one loan denial

WORKED EXAMPLE — SHAP on a single prediction
Applicant denied at score 0.31 (threshold 0.5). SHAP attributes the gap from the base rate (0.6): debt-to-income −0.18, recent delinquency −0.09, short credit history −0.05, income +0.03. The explanation: “primarily debt-to-income and the recent delinquency” — auditable, actionable, and required for consequential decisions.
Toolbox: SHAP (game-theoretic, local+global), LIME (local surrogate), permutation importance (global), attention/saliency maps (deep nets), counterfactuals (“approved if income +$8k”). Interpretable-by-design (logistic/trees) vs post-hoc explanation of black boxes is the standing trade.
⚠️ LOCAL vs GLOBAL
“Why THIS prediction?” → local (SHAP/LIME per instance). “What drives the model overall?” → global (importances). Matching question-to-scope is the repeated exam item.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

If you cannot explain why your model made a decision, you cannot debug it, defend it in court, or build user trust. Explainability tools turn black boxes into things humans can reason about.

Core concepts

1. Interpretable vs explainable. Interpretable: model is inherently understandable (linear regression, small trees). Explainable: black-box model with post-hoc explanations (SHAP, LIME). Different goals.

2. SHAP values. Game-theoretic feature attribution. Each feature gets a value showing its contribution to a specific prediction. Sums to (prediction − baseline). The current standard for explanations.

3. LIME. Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations. Fits a simple linear model around a single prediction. Useful for instance-level explanations.

4. Model cards and datasheets. Standardized documentation. Model card: intended use, performance per group, limitations. Datasheet: dataset provenance, collection process, biases.

5. Communicating uncertainty. Show confidence scores, calibration plots, error bars. Users handle uncertainty better when it is shown explicitly than when it is hidden.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Treating SHAP as ground truth — it explains the model, not the world. The model can be wrong about causation.
  • Skipping model cards because they are tedious — until something goes wrong and there is no documentation.
  • Using explanations to justify decisions rather than question them — confirmation bias risk.

Quick recap

Explainability spans inherently interpretable models and post-hoc tools (SHAP, LIME). Document with model cards and datasheets. Communicate uncertainty honestly.

Glossary

SHAP
SHapley Additive exPlanations; per-feature contribution to a prediction.
Model card
Structured doc describing model intent, performance, and limits.
Counterfactual
What would change the model's decision; useful for explanation.

The Limitations section of a model card should HONESTLY state where the model fails or is uncertain — populations, conditions, and inputs it handles poorly. A model card that only advertises is marketing, not documentation.

📊 FIGURE — translating an explanation for its audience
🎯 EXAM TIP
When presenting SHAP to non-technical stakeholders, translate into business terms and simplify. "Income contributed +0.23 to the log-odds" is not an explanation to a loan officer; "this application scored lower mainly because of the short credit history" is.
"}, "D683/ch6/s4": {"title": "AI Safety and Adversarial Robustness", "body": "
📖 DEFINITIONS AT A GLANCE — key terms in this section
TermDefinition
Adversarial exampleInput crafted to fool a model with minimal change.
Prompt injectionHidden instructions in input that hijack an LLM.
Defense-in-depthMultiple overlapping defenses; no single point of failure.
Full lesson with examples below ⬇️ — nothing removed.

📖 Worked example — adversarial robustness & safety layers

WORKED EXAMPLE — attack, then defend
Attack (FGSM idea): take the panda image, compute the gradient of the loss w.r.t. PIXELS, nudge every pixel a hair in the loss-increasing direction (ε so small humans see no change) → the classifier now says “gibbon” at 99%. Same trick physically: stickers on stop signs.
Defenses: adversarial training (train on attacked examples — the workhorse), input preprocessing, certified bounds (provable radius), detection of adversarial inputs.
LLM safety adds: prompt injection/jailbreaks (inputs that override instructions) → input/output filtering, system-prompt hardening, red-teaming; alignment training (RLHF) to refuse harmful requests; misuse monitoring.
⚠️ IMPERCEPTIBLE ≠ HARMLESS
